extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics majors (students in an introduction-to-proofs / MATH 300 style course) and instructors using such a course text
extracted.subtask_description: A college-level textbook introducing sets, logic, counting, and common proof techniques (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction, etc.), with exercises and instructor guidance for a semester-long proofs course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and notation for sets
rubrics_metrics.description: A set is a collection of things; elements are denoted with ∈; sets are often written with braces { ... }; special named sets include N, Z, Q, R; the empty set is ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use uppercase letters to name sets and write membership as x ∈ A. Be careful distinguishing ∅ and {0}: ∅ has no elements while {0} contains one element (the number 0). Provide examples (finite and infinite sets) and apply the box analogy to visualize sets and elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-builder notation
rubrics_metrics.description: When sets are too large or complex to list, write X = {expression : rule} to denote all values of 'expression' satisfying 'rule'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the colon as 'such that'. Give multiple equivalent forms (e.g., {2n : n ∈ Z} = {n ∈ Z : n is even}). Use examples and note potential notational conflicts (e.g., |x| meaning absolute value vs cardinality depending on context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality and power sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is finite, |A| denotes its number of elements; the power set P(A) (denoted ^(A) in the text) is the set of all subsets of A and has size 2^{|A|}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrate with examples (e.g., P({1,2,3})). Emphasize that infinite sets have power sets too (e.g., P(R^2) contains graphs of every function, black-and-white images, etc.) and discuss the mind-boggling size of P(R^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartesian product and ordered tuples
rubrics_metrics.description: Define ordered pair (x,y) and Cartesian product A×B = {(a,b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B}. Extend to ordered triples and A^n for Cartesian powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagrams (rows/columns) to visualize finite AxB. Warn about parentheses/associativity distinctions (R × (N × Z) elements look like (x,(y,z)) vs R × N × Z elements as (x,y,z)). Give examples (R×R = plane).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subset relations and counting subsets
rubrics_metrics.description: A ⊆ B means every element of A is in B; ∅ ⊆ B for any set B; a finite set with n elements has 2^n subsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach listing subsets via a branching/tree method. Use concrete examples to help students distinguish between elements that are sets vs numbers (e.g., {1} vs 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Union, intersection, difference, and complement
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce AuB = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B}, AnB = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}, A - B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B}, and complements relative to a universal set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interval examples and plane sketches (graphs) to illustrate operations. Provide De Morgan style identities implicitly (index lists them). Show examples where order of difference matters (A-B ≠ B-A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful use of notation and contextual meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Notation can be overloaded; e.g., |x| denotes absolute value when x is a number but cardinality when x is a set; (a,b) can denote an ordered pair or an open interval depending on context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always ensure context clarifies meaning. Provide examples contrasting the two uses and highlight common pitfalls (bars, parentheses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements, logical connectives, and truth tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Define mathematical statements and logical connectives (and, or, not) and evaluate them using truth tables; introduce logical equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include truth-table exercises and examples showing equivalences. Emphasize building correct logical structure before proving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional statements and contrapositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditional statements have form 'If P then Q'. The contrapositive 'If not Q then not P' is logically equivalent and can be used as a proof technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach when contrapositive is more convenient than direct proof (e.g., in certain integer congruence arguments). Give examples (see chapter on congruence of integers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional (if-and-only-if) proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove 'P iff Q' by proving both directions: P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P (or by showing equivalence through a chain of logically equivalent statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present structured approaches for IFF proofs and exercises to practice rearranging and proving equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translating English to symbolic logic and quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach translation of ordinary-language mathematical claims into logical formulas using universal and existential quantifiers; demonstrate correct negation of quantified statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include many translation and negation exercises and discuss common language traps. Emphasize clarity with quantifier order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof technique
rubrics_metrics.description: For statements of form 'If P then Q', derive Q from the assumption P using definitions, algebra, and previously established results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover writing clear theorems and definitions first (see sections on Theorems and Definitions). Show use of cases and treating similar cases carefully. Provide many examples and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contrapositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove 'If P then Q' by proving its contrapositive 'If not Q then not P' when that route is simpler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include worked examples (e.g., congruence of integers) and note when this method avoids awkward direct manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the negation of the desired statement and derive a contradiction to conclude the original statement is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover variations: proving conditional statements via contradiction, combining techniques, and provide 'Some words of advice' about when contradiction is appropriate (see chapter 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical writing and exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for writing proofs: clarity, correct notation, logical flow, and sufficient explanation so readers can follow each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contains a dedicated section (5.3) on mathematical writing: use clear definitions, state hypotheses, avoid ambiguous notation, and present proofs in readable steps. Exercises and examples illustrate good vs poor practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: If-and-only-if proofs, equivalent statements, and existence proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques for proving non-conditional statements: construct equivalences, prove existence by example or constructive method, and handle uniqueness when required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide templates: for existence, give an explicit example; for IFF, prove both directions; for equivalence, show chain of implications or mutual implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof via counterexample and disproof techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove universal or existence claims, provide counterexamples or show contradiction from assumed universality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize constructing explicit counterexamples for false statements and explain disproof by contradiction for existence statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical induction (standard, strong, and smallest counterexample)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove statements about integers by base case plus inductive step (standard), by assuming all smaller cases (strong), or by assuming a smallest counterexample and deriving contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include variants and examples (e.g., Fibonacci numbers). Show when strong induction or smallest-counterexample method is more natural. Provide careful structure for inductive proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to prove set-theoretic claims (a ∈ A, A ⊆ B, A = B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific recipes: to prove a ∈ A show construction or rule that yields a; to prove A ⊆ B take arbitrary x ∈ A and show x ∈ B; to prove A = B show both A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 8 gives targeted advice and examples; use element-chasing and clear quantifier handling. Give sample proofs (e.g., proving subset equalities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations, equivalence relations, and partitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Define relations and properties (reflexive, symmetric, transitive); equivalence relations induce equivalence classes and partitions of the underlying set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include examples (integers modulo n), exercises to check properties, and explanations of equivalence classes and their connection to partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions: domain, codomain, injective/surjective, composition, inverse, image/preimage
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal definitions of functions and their properties; composition and inverses; image f(X) and preimage f^{-1}(Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide methods for proving injectivity (one-to-one) and surjectivity (onto), for constructing inverses, and for manipulating images/preimages with set operations (with proofs/exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole principle and counting techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting principles including lists, factorials, binomial coefficients, inclusion-exclusion, and the pigeonhole principle for existence conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use worked examples and combinatorial arguments (e.g., remainder/pigeonhole proofs). Provide exercises applying these techniques to prove divisibility or existence claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality comparisons: countable vs uncountable and bijections
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare sizes via bijections; define countable sets (finite or bijective with N) and uncountable sets; demonstrate techniques to show equal cardinalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constructive bijections and classical arguments (e.g., diagonalization implicitly elsewhere) and provide numerous examples/exercises showing |R| = |(0,∞)| etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course and textbook production guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbook intended to be covered in a 14-week semester; chapters and sections are suggested for scheduling; new editions issued only to correct mistakes/clarify exposition and not to renumber exercises arbitrarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a suggested three-day-per-week timetable mapping sections to weeks. Preface notes editorial policy (minor clarifications only) and inclusion of solutions for instructors/students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises with worked solutions and progressive practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Each section includes exercises designed to practice concepts and proof techniques; solutions are provided later in the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises range from straightforward notation/translation tasks to proof construction and counterexample finding. Solutions illustrate expected style and correctness; use them to learn structure of good proofs.
